title: Computer Science
content: Computer science is the study of computation, information processes, and the design of hardware and software [[dead_link|systems]]. The field encompasses [[dead_link|algorithms]], programming languages, machine learning, and theoretical models of [[dead_link|computation]]. Modern interdisciplinary branches connect computing to linguistics ([[cl|Computational Linguistics]]), humanities scholarship ([[dh|Digital Humanities]]), and historical analysis of early computing devices ([[hoc|History of Computing]]).

title: History of Computing
content: History of computing examines the development of computational devices and methodologies from ancient counting tools to modern [[dead_link|information machines]]. It studies innovations such as ([[mcd|Mechanical Calculating Devices]]), early encryption systems ([[ec|Early Cryptography]]), and foundational theories shaping modern [[cs|Computer Science]].

title: Mechanical Calculating Devices
content: Mechanical calculating devices are early tools designed to automate arithmetic using gears, levers, and clockwork [[dead_link|mechanisms]]. These machines influenced both real historical development and fictional constructs such as [[ab|Automaton Birds]], and remain central artifacts in the broader [[hoc|History of Computing]].

title: Early Cryptography
content: Early cryptography refers to pre-modern systems of encoding messages, including substitution ciphers, polyalphabetic schemes, and mechanical [[dead_link|cipher wheels]]. The field is linked to mysterious encoded texts such as ([[cm|Cipher Manuscripts]]) and also to literary studies involving [[pc|Poe and Cryptography]].

title: Computational Linguistics
content: Computational linguistics combines linguistics and computer science to model human language with [[dead_link|computational models]]. Applications include text parsing, authorship identification, and semantic analysis, topics that overlap with ([[sty|Stylometry]]) and interdisciplinary research in [[dh|Digital Humanities]].

title: Stylometry
content: Stylometry is the quantitative study of linguistic style using statistical and [[dead_link|machine-based]] methods. It is used in authorship attribution, historical text analysis, and investigations involving coded or disputed works, often connecting to ([[lf|Literary Forensics]]) and studies of [[pc|Poe and Cryptography]].

title: Literary Forensics
content: Literary forensics applies analytical and scientific techniques to literature to assess authorship, authenticity, and textual [[dead_link|integrity]]. The discipline frequently examines works within ([[agl|American Gothic Literature]]) and employs stylistic tools derived from [[sty|Stylometry]].

title: Digital Humanities
content: Digital humanities integrates computational tools with humanistic research, enabling large-scale text mining, digital archiving, and interactive [[dead_link|scholarly platforms]]. Practitioners work with digital genres such as ([[el|Electronic Literature]]) and preserve unusual or fragile works within the ([[aot|Archive of Obscure Texts]]).

title: Electronic Literature
content: Electronic literature comprises digital-native works that use computational, multimedia, or interactive [[dead_link|structures]]. The genre includes hypertext narratives such as ([[hf|Hypertext Fiction]]) and is often studied alongside digital archiving efforts like the [[aot|Archive of Obscure Texts]].

title: Archive of Obscure Texts
content: The Archive of Obscure Texts is a fictional digital repository dedicated to rare, fragmentary, or enigmatic [[dead_link|documents]]. Its collections include encoded works such as ([[cm|Cipher Manuscripts]]) and historical publications featured in ([[fp19|Forgotten Periodicals of the 19th Century]]), making it an important resource within [[dh|Digital Humanities]].

title: Cipher Manuscripts
content: Cipher manuscripts are texts written using symbolic or coded systems designed to resist straightforward [[dead_link|interpretation]]. They attract scholars of [[ec|Early Cryptography]] and are preserved in fictional archives like the [[aot|Archive of Obscure Texts]], frequently intersecting with studies of [[pc|Poe and Cryptography]].

title: Poe and Cryptography
content: Poe and cryptography refers to [[eap|Edgar Allan Poe]]'s interest in puzzles, cryptograms, and linguistic [[dead_link|riddles]]. His essays and challenges influenced later cryptographic studies and are often analyzed in relation to [[ec|Early Cryptography]], stylistic methods in [[sty|Stylometry]], and literary tradition in [[agl|American Gothic Literature]].

title: American Gothic Literature
content: American Gothic literature explores darkness, psychological tension, and supernatural [[dead_link|motifs]] in U.S. settings. Writers such as [[eap|Edgar Allan Poe]] helped define the genre, which is examined in analytical disciplines including [[lf|Literary Forensics]].

title: Forgotten Periodicals of the 19th Century
content: Forgotten Periodicals of the 19th Century refers to obscure magazines and short-lived publications featuring serialized fiction, puzzles, and experimental [[dead_link|narratives]]. These works are often connected to cryptographic documents within the [[aot|Archive of Obscure Texts]] and sometimes relate to writings by [[eap|Edgar Allan Poe]].

title: Edgar Allan Poe
content: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer, poet, and critic known for his contributions to [[dead_link|detective fiction]] and macabre storytelling. His works are foundational within [[agl|American Gothic Literature]], and his fascination with cryptography is widely examined in ([[pc|Poe and Cryptography]]).
